new.title: Stand under the five domes of Saint-Front cathedral
new.desc: The Romanesque-Byzantine Cathédrale Saint-Front rises above the old town with five domes on pendentives, heavily restored by Paul Abadie in the 19th century. It became the cathedral in 1669 and is a major stage on the Saint-Jacques-de-Compostelle routes.
new.tip: Entry is free. Walk up from the Isle quays for the classic view of the domes.
new.q: Cathédrale Saint-Front, Place de la Clautre, Périgueux

new.title: Walk over a Roman domus at Vesunna museum
new.desc: Vesunna, designed by architect Jean Nouvel and opened in 2003, is built over the remains of a large, well-preserved Gallo-Roman house in the Parc de Vésone. Displays include an altar to Cybele, a relief of Mercury and a garum amphora.
new.tip: Closed Mondays; check hours on the official site. Combine with the Tour de Vésone a few minutes away.
new.q: Vesunna Site-musée gallo-romain, 20 Rue du 26e Régiment d'Infanterie, Périgueux

new.title: See the Tour de Vésone, a 2nd-century Roman cella
new.desc: The 25 m Tour de Vésone is the surviving cella of a Gallo-Roman temple to the tutelary goddess of Vesunna, built in the 2nd century AD. It has been a listed monument since 1846.
new.tip: Free to view from the park beside the Vesunna museum; best in late afternoon light.
new.q: Tour de Vésone, Rue Claude Bernard, Périgueux

new.title: Stroll the Jardin des Arènes over a Roman amphitheatre
new.desc: A public garden laid out in the 19th century covers the remains of Vesunna's Roman amphitheatre, with several metres of fill hiding most of the arena. Panels explain the arena's construction and role.
new.tip: Free and open; a shady stop between Vesunna and the old town.
new.q: Jardin des Arènes, Boulevard des Arènes, Périgueux

new.title: Wander the Puy-Saint-Front lanes to Maison des Dames de la Foi
new.desc: The Puy-Saint-Front quarter around rue Limogeanne keeps Renaissance houses from Périgueux's prosperous 16th century. The medieval Maison des Dames de la Foi on rue des Farges, first recorded in 1247 as a Templar house, has pointed arches and a loggia.
new.tip: Walk rue des Farges, rue Limogeanne and the Maison du Pâtissier together; pick up the town plan at the tourist office.
new.q: Maison des Dames de la Foi, 4 Rue des Farges, Périgueux

new.title: Trace 70,000 years at the MAAP museum
new.desc: The Musée d'art et d'archéologie du Périgord occupies a former Augustinian monastery and shows over 2,000 m² of permanent collections from prehistory through the Roman and medieval periods. It is a Musée de France.
new.tip: Located on cours Tourny; check the site for exhibition changes.
new.q: Musée d'art et d'archéologie du Périgord, 22 Cours Tourny, Périgueux

new.title: Climb the Tour Mataguerre for old-town rooftops
new.desc: The 13th-century Tour Mataguerre is the only survivor of the 28 towers of Périgueux's town wall. Short guided visites flash climb to the top for views over the old town.
new.tip: Access is by guided visit booked through the tourist office on place du Coderc.
new.q: Tour Mataguerre, Rue de la Bride, Périgueux

new.title: Find the old cathedral of Saint-Étienne-de-la-Cité
new.desc: Built from the 11th century on the site of a temple to Mars, this was Périgueux's cathedral until 1669. Wars of Religion destroyed its belfry and two of its four domes, leaving two of the original domes standing.
new.tip: A short walk from the Vesunna museum; combine both for the Roman-to-medieval story.
new.q: Église Saint-Étienne-de-la-Cité, Rue de la Cité, Périgueux

new.title: Shop foie gras and truffle at Maison Requier
new.desc: Maison Requier on rue de la Sagesse is a delicatessen in the centre of Périgueux selling Périgord classics: foie gras, pâtés, fritons and truffles. Gault&Millau lists it among the city's artisan food addresses.
new.tip: Buy a jar of foie gras mi-cuit or truffle products to take home; closed Sundays typically, so check.
new.q: Maison Requier, 8 Rue de la Sagesse, Périgueux

new.title: Eat duck breast with Périgueux sauce at Hercule Poireau
new.desc: This restaurant sits at the foot of Saint-Front cathedral in a 16th-century vaulted room. Its menu includes scallops, foie gras, duck breast with Périgueux sauce and sweetbreads, and it has a Michelin Plate mention.
new.tip: Book ahead in the evening; order foie gras with a glass of Monbazillac.
new.q: Hercule Poireau, 2 Rue de la Nation, Périgueux

new.title: Taste the tarte aux noix at Antoine Girard
new.desc: Antoine Girard is a boulangerie-pâtisserie in Périgueux praised by critic Gilles Pudlowski for its tarte aux noix and tourte Saint-Georges. It also bakes a gâteau aux noix du Périgord, using the region's AOP walnuts.
new.tip: Go in the morning for the fullest counter; walnut tart travels well.
new.q: Antoine Girard Pâtisserie Boulangerie, 41 Boulevard de Stalingrad, Périgueux

new.title: Dine on roast foie gras at La Taula
new.desc: La Taula, near the cathedral, serves modern Périgord cooking: roast duck foie gras with four spices, foie gras carpaccio with hazelnut oil and veal kidneys with mustard seed.
new.tip: Reserve ahead; the tourist office listing gives current opening days.
new.q: La Taula, Rue de la Clarté, Périgueux

new.title: Browse the Wednesday and Saturday market
new.desc: The Périgueux market spreads over place de la Clautre, place du Coderc and place Saint-Silain on Wednesday and Saturday mornings. Stalls sell local produce, walnuts, cheese and duck products.
new.tip: Wednesday and Saturday, roughly 8:00 to 13:00; arrive early for the best choice.

new.title: Visit the winter foie gras market on Place Saint-Louis
new.desc: Each winter producers of foie gras, confit and magret sell on place Saint-Louis, in the shadow of the old town's Renaissance houses. It runs on Wednesday and Saturday mornings from November to March.
new.tip: Wednesdays and Saturdays, 8:30 to 13:00, November to March; exact dates are announced each autumn.

new.title: Walk or cycle the Isle riverbank voie verte
new.desc: The voie verte des berges de l'Isle runs through Périgueux along the river, open to walkers, cyclists and skaters. A short stroll from the Quais de l'Isle car park gives a full view of Saint-Front cathedral.
new.tip: Free parking at the Quais de l'Isle; the Marsac to Périgueux stretch is about 15 km one way.

new.title: Join a guided food tour of Périgueux
new.desc: The tourist office offers a balade gourmande through the old town, tasting regional products with a guide. It highlights the city's gastronomic history around the Saint-Front quarter.
new.tip: Book through the Périgueux tourist office on place du Coderc; seasonal.
new.q: Office de Tourisme Destination Périgueux, 9 bis Place du Coderc, Périgueux

new.title: Descend into the Lascaux IV cave replica
new.desc: Lascaux IV, designed by Snøhetta and completed in 2016, is a full replica of the Lascaux cave in Montignac, with the 1,900 paintings and engravings recreated using the original pigments. The original cave was found on 8 September 1940.
new.tip: Allow 2.5 to 3 hours and book timed tickets online; the replica stays at about 13 degrees.
new.q: Lascaux IV, Avenue de Lascaux, Montignac-Lascaux

new.title: Book Font-de-Gaume for original polychrome bison
new.desc: Font-de-Gaume near Les Eyzies is one of the last decorated caves in France where you can see original polychrome Magdalenian paintings. Groups are limited to 13 people.
new.tip: Online booking only, weeks ahead in summer; the visit lasts 1h30 to 2h with part outdoors.
new.q: Grotte de Font-de-Gaume, Route de Sarlat, Les Eyzies

new.title: Ride the electric train in Rouffignac cave
new.desc: The Grotte de Rouffignac, the Cave of the Hundred Mammoths, has about eight kilometres of galleries and Magdalenian art around 15,000 years old. A small electric train has carried visitors through it since 1959.
new.tip: Visits are guided; the cave is cool, so bring a jacket.

new.title: Explore the Musée national de Préhistoire
new.desc: The museum in Les Eyzies, founded by Denis Peyrony, covers over 400,000 years of human presence in the Vézère valley. Its collections trace hominid chronology and prehistoric art.
new.tip: Combined discounts exist with Abri Pataud; check musee-prehistoire-eyzies.fr for hours.
new.q: Musée national de Préhistoire, 1 Rue du Musée, Les Eyzies

new.title: Tour the excavated Abri Pataud shelter
new.desc: The Abri Pataud in Les Eyzies preserves 14 layers of occupation between about 35,000 and 25,000 years ago, with an on-site museum and visible excavations. Finds include an ibex engraving and a young woman's skull.
new.tip: Guided visits; a reduced Musée national de Préhistoire ticket is offered on presentation of the Pataud ticket.
new.q: Abri Pataud, 20 Rue du Moyen-Age, Les Eyzies

new.title: Climb La Roque Saint-Christophe's cliff city
new.desc: A kilometre-long limestone cliff at Peyzac-le-Moustier holds a troglodyte fort and medieval city, inhabited for around 55,000 years. It has been open to visitors since 1952 and is protected as a historic monument.
new.tip: Open year-round with free and guided visits; wear sturdy shoes.

new.title: Lose yourself in Sarlat's medieval centre
new.desc: Sarlat-la-Canéda's old town is among France's best-preserved medieval towns, with honey-coloured stone lanes and the square of Place des Oies with its bronze geese by François-Xavier Lalanne. The 12th-century Lanterne des Morts rises behind the cathedral.
new.tip: Visit early or after dark when day crowds thin; the Lanterne is viewed from the jardin des Enfeus.
new.q: Place du Marché aux Oies, Sarlat-la-Canéda

new.title: Climb the cliff-top Château de Beynac
new.desc: The medieval Château de Beynac stands on a cliff above the Dordogne with a keep viewpoint over the valley and its castles. It has appeared in many films.
new.tip: Allow 1h30 to 2h; closed shoes recommended. Park at the top of the village.
new.q: Château de Beynac, Place du Château, Beynac-et-Cazenac

new.title: See trebuchets at Castelnaud's medieval war museum
new.desc: The Château de Castelnaud houses the Musée de la Guerre au Moyen Âge, with nearly 300 weapons and suits of armour and full-size siege engines including a trebuchet. Demonstrations are staged in season.
new.tip: Check castelnaud.com for demonstration times; views across to Beynac from the ramparts.

new.title: See La Roque-Gageac squeezed under its cliff
new.desc: The village of La Roque-Gageac is built into a cliff above the Dordogne, with troglodyte dwellings still visible. It draws over a million visitors a year to a population of under 500.
new.tip: Walk the riverside road, then look up at the cliff houses; park outside the village in summer.

new.title: Wander Bergerac's old town to Place Pélissière
new.desc: Bergerac's protected old town has half-timbered houses from the 15th to 17th centuries around Place Pélissière, where a Cyrano statue stands since 2005. The Église Saint-Jacques and Maison Peyrarède, home to the Musée du Tabac, are close by.
new.tip: A loop of the old town takes about 1 to 2 hours; stop at a café on the square.

new.title: Visit the double château of Bourdeilles
new.desc: The Château de Bourdeilles combines a 13th-century medieval fortress with an elegant Renaissance dwelling beside the Dronne. It has been a listed monument since 1919 and has a French garden.
new.tip: Hours vary by season; theatrical evening visits run in summer.
new.q: Château de Bourdeilles, Place de la Halle, Bourdeilles

new.title: Discover Saint-Jean-de-Côle and its Romano-Byzantine church
new.desc: Saint-Jean-de-Côle is a Plus Beaux Villages de France with a Romano-Byzantine priory church and the Château de la Marthonie around its central square. The château is largely 15th to 17th century and open in summer by reservation.
new.tip: The village is free to wander; castle visits go through the tourist office in summer.

new.title: Tour Château de Hautefort and its gardens
new.desc: Hautefort's château is surrounded by more than three hectares of French formal gardens and an English-style park, both classed as Jardins Remarquables. Several guided and self-guided ticket combinations are offered.
new.tip: Guided tours may need booking; wear comfortable shoes for park paths.

new.title: Visit Joséphine Baker's Château des Milandes
new.desc: Joséphine Baker bought the Château des Milandes in 1947 and lived there until she was expelled in 1968. The visit tells the château's story and Baker's life, with gardens and birds of prey shows.
new.tip: Raptor shows are seasonal; check milandes.com for the schedule.

new.title: Climb the Grand Escalier to Rocamadour's sanctuary
new.desc: Rocamadour clings to a cliff, with its pilgrim sanctuary reached by the Grand Escalier. The Chapelle Notre-Dame holds a wooden Black Madonna and the sanctuary is part of the UNESCO Santiago routes.
new.tip: Elevators run for a fee; a sword said to be Durandal is wedged in the rock nearby.

new.title: See Pech Merle's 20,000-year-old paintings
new.desc: The Grotte du Pech Merle in Cabrerets has paintings more than 20,000 years old, discovered in 1922 by two teenagers. Visits are guided in groups of up to 25.
new.tip: Book at pechmerle.com; visitor numbers are capped for conservation.

new.title: Read the world's scripts at the Champollion museum
new.desc: The Musée Champollion – Les Écritures du Monde in Figeac sits in the house where Champollion was born. Reopened in 2007, it covers the history of writing worldwide and holds the Musée de France label.
new.tip: On place Champollion; a 2026 exhibition on Hangeul runs until 11 October.

new.title: Cross the fortified Pont Valentré in Cahors
new.desc: Begun in 1308, the six-span Pont Valentré over the Lot took about 70 years to finish and has become Cahors's symbol. Vehicles are not allowed and it is lit at night.
new.tip: Walk across at dusk when it is illuminated; free at all times.

new.title: Admire Carennac's Romanesque tympan and cloister
new.desc: The village of Carennac grew around a Cluniac priory whose church has a 12th-century tympan. The cloister is half Romanesque, half Gothic and holds a late-15th-century entombment.
new.tip: Combine with Autoire and Loubressac on a drive through the Dordogne valley villages.

new.title: See three valleys from Loubressac
new.desc: Loubressac, a Plus Beaux Villages de France since 1983, sits at 354 m with views over the Dordogne, Cère and Bave valleys. Its 14th-century castle and Saint-Jean-Baptiste church stand among flowered lanes.
new.tip: Photographer Robert Doisneau reportedly admired the light here; go late afternoon.

new.title: Descend into the crystal cathedral of Proumeyssac
new.desc: The Gouffre de Proumeyssac in Audrix, discovered in 1907, is nicknamed the Cathédrale de Cristal for its petrifying fountain and triangular crystals. An optional basket descent gives a 360-degree view.
new.tip: Open all year except January; book the nacelle descent, limited to 11 people.

new.title: Glide by boat on the Padirac underground river
new.desc: The Gouffre de Padirac has been open to the public since 1898 after Édouard-Alfred Martel's 1889 exploration. Visitors board boats in groups of 11 for roughly 500 m on the underground river.
new.tip: Book a timed slot in season; the cave is cool and damp.

new.title: Walk the box-hedge paths at Marqueyssac
new.desc: The Jardins de Marqueyssac hold about 150,000 hand-clipped boxwoods across 22 hectares, with over 6 km of paths to the Belvédère de la Dordogne, 130 m above the river. Candlelit evenings run on Thursdays in July and August.
new.tip: Hours and prices vary by season; check marqueyssac.com.

new.title: Walk Domme's bastide to the Belvédère de la Barre
new.desc: The bastide of Domme, founded in 1281 under Philip III, sits on a 150 m cliff. The Belvédère de la Barre looks toward the Montfort meander and La Roque-Gageac, and the town's grotte is accessible from the halle.
new.tip: The belvédère is free; cave tours are guided and cost around 8.50 euros in summer.

new.title: Stroll Brantôme's abbey, pont coudé and Jardin des Moines
new.desc: Brantôme sits on an island in the Dronne and is called the Venise du Périgord. The Benedictine abbey, traditionally founded in 769, backs onto cliff caves, and the L-shaped pont coudé leads to the Jardin des Moines.
new.tip: Do the loop on foot in an hour or two; the village is also a good lunch stop.
new.q: Abbaye de Brantôme, Brantôme en Périgord

new.title: Paddle a canoe from Vézac past Castelnaud and Beynac
new.desc: Operators at Vézac such as Canoës Découverte run circuits of 5 to 28 km on the Dordogne, past castles and cliffs. Couleurs Périgord offers 5 to 20 km descents passing Montfort, Domme, Castelnaud and Beynac.
new.tip: Typically April to October; swimmers need to swim 25 m on some routes. Check prices with the operator.
new.q: Canoës Découverte, 508 Route des Gabarres, Vézac

new.title: Take a gabare boat trip on the Dordogne
new.desc: Replica gabares, traditional flat-bottomed boats, leave La Roque-Gageac for commented trips past the village and the Malartrie château. Operators include Gabares Norbert and Gabarres Caminade.
new.tip: Rides run April to early November and not on flood days; about an hour.
new.q: Gabares Norbert, Place du 8 Mai, La Roque-Gageac

new.title: Shop Sarlat's Saturday market
new.desc: On Saturday mornings the market fills Sarlat's old centre, from rue de la République to place des Oies, with walnuts, goat cheeses and confit jars. There is also a Wednesday morning market.
new.tip: Food stalls run roughly 8:00 to 13:00; the market is sometimes moved during Fest'oie and the truffle festival.

new.title: Join Sarlat Fest'Oie, the goose festival
new.desc: Every first weekend of March the Fest'Oie fills Place de la Liberté with goose-themed events: cooking classes, producer stands, a Bodeg'Oie evening and a banquet of 15 goose dishes. It has run since 2009; the next is 6 to 7 March 2027.
new.tip: Animations are free; the banquet needs a paid reservation and sells out fast.

new.title: Hunt truffles at the Écomusée de la Truffe in Sorges
new.desc: The Écomusée de la Truffe at Sorges has a truffle trail across the limestone causse and guided tastings. Truffle hunting demonstrations with a dog happen in season, and black truffle is harvested from mid-November to mid-March.
new.tip: Book guided visits and cavage in advance; Sorges also holds a Sunday truffle market.
new.q: Écomusée de la Truffe, 2 Route des Truffières, Sorges

new.title: Hike to the Autoire waterfall and cirque
new.desc: Autoire sits in a limestone cirque with cliffs of 150 to 200 m and a waterfall of about 30 m. A trail of around 1.2 km from the village car park leads to the falls; longer loops link Loubressac.
new.tip: Wear grippy shoes as paths can be slippery; Siran hamlet gives a panoramic view.

new.title: Climb Saint-Cirq-Lapopie above the Lot
new.desc: Saint-Cirq-Lapopie perches on a cliff of roughly 100 m above the Lot, with thirteen listed buildings and a fortified church. It was voted favourite village of the French in 2012 and André Breton lived here from 1950.
new.tip: Go early or late to avoid the crowds; about 400,000 visitors come each year.

new.title: Walk the Lot towpath from Bouziès to Saint-Cirq
new.desc: The chemin de halage links Bouziès to Saint-Cirq-Lapopie, about 10 km, flat to the Ganil lock, where haulers cut the path into the cliff in 1847. A short climb finishes at the village.
new.tip: Park at the chemin de halage car park at Bouziès; busy in summer.

new.title: Browse Cahors's Wednesday and Saturday market
new.desc: Cahors's outdoor market runs on Wednesday and Saturday mornings around the Saint-Étienne cathedral and alongside the covered Halle, open Tuesday to Saturday. Works have moved the Saturday market to the allées Fénelon.
new.tip: Check the current location with the tourist office as it has shifted during works.

new.title: Order foie gras terrine at Le Présidial in Sarlat
new.desc: Le Présidial, created in 1999 on rue Landry in the old quarter, serves mi-cuit duck foie gras terrine with onion confit and spiced red wine, plus magret dishes.
new.tip: Closed Sundays and some lunches; book ahead.

new.title: Taste seasonal Périgord cuisine at L'Imparfait
new.desc: L'Imparfait on rue des Fontaines in Bergerac is a Michelin-listed restaurant in a stone setting with a semi-open kitchen. Chef Hervé Battiston cooks seasonal terroir dishes; Gault&Millau rates it 12/20.
new.tip: Menus range roughly 29 to 85 euros; reserve in the evening.

new.title: Eat creative bistro plates at La Table du Marché
new.desc: La Table du Marché on place Louis de la Bardonnie in Bergerac is a creative French bistro with a 2025 Michelin Plate.
new.tip: Book for dinner; confirm opening days locally.
new.q: La Table du Marché, Place Louis de la Bardonnie, Bergerac

new.title: Taste Monbazillac sweet wine at the château
new.desc: The 16th-century Château de Monbazillac offers a visit with a tasting of its liquoreux wines, from one-wine to three-wine commented formulas. It is among the world's largest sweet-wine estates.
new.tip: Allow at least 1h30; open daily 10:00 to 20:00 in July and August.

new.title: Splurge on a truffle tasting menu at Charbonnel
new.desc: Hôtel-Restaurant Charbonnel on rue Gambetta in Brantôme offers 3, 5 or 7-course tasting menus with truffle, foie gras and caviar. Gault&Millau rates it 13/20 and Michelin lists it as creative cuisine.
new.tip: Reserve ahead; dinner is a splurge.
new.q: Hôtel-Restaurant Charbonnel, 57 Rue Gambetta, Brantôme en Périgord

new.title: Eat pâté en croûte at the Moulin de l'Abbaye
new.desc: La Table du Moulin de l'Abbaye, in a riverside hotel in Brantôme, is the town's best-known dining address. A pâté en croûte with foie gras and Périgord truffle is among its dishes.
new.tip: Ask for a table by the river; check seasonal opening.
new.q: Le Moulin de l'Abbaye, 1 Route de Bourdeilles, Brantôme en Périgord

new.title: Taste walnut oil at Moulin de la Veyssière
new.desc: The Moulin de la Veyssière in Neuvic has pressed walnut oil since the 16th century and the Elias family has run it since 1857. It is the last working oil mill of the Vern valley and also makes hazelnut and almond oils.
new.tip: The visit and tasting are free, every 30 minutes; closed Sundays.
new.q: Moulin de la Veyssière, 819 Route de la Veyssière, Neuvic

new.title: Buy Rocamadour AOP goat cheese at Étoile du Quercy
new.desc: The Fromagerie Étoile du Quercy was founded in Loubressac by Francis Verdier in 1986 and makes Rocamadour AOP plus goat and sheep milk specialities. Rocamadour is a small raw-goat's-milk cheese from the Causses du Quercy.
new.tip: Check the 2026 opening hours listed on the Occitanie tourism page.

new.title: Taste Cahors Malbec at Clos de Gamot
new.desc: The Jouffreau family's Clos de Gamot in Prayssac is a historic Cahors Malbec estate; much of the Cahors vineyard was replanted with clones from its vines after phylloxera.
new.tip: Tastings are listed with the Occitanie tourism board; call ahead.

new.title: Try Quercy tradition at L'Ô à la Bouche in Cahors
new.desc: L'Ô à la Bouche in Cahors serves cooking rooted in Quercy tradition; Gault&Millau rates it 12.5/20 and cites semi-cooked duck foie gras with green apple. Michelin lists it as modern cuisine.
new.tip: Book ahead for dinner; pair with a Cahors Malbec.
new.q: L'Ô à la Bouche, Rue Saint-Urcisse, Cahors

new.title: Eat Quercy lamb at La Dînée du Viguier in Figeac
new.desc: La Dînée du Viguier, the bistronomic restaurant of the Mercure Figeac Viguier du Roy, cooks with Quercy and Lot products; signature dishes reportedly include Quercy lamb with confit shoulder.
new.tip: Reserve for dinner.
new.q: La Dînée du Viguier, 4 Rue Boutaric, Figeac

new.title: Lunch at the bistro Au Fil du Temps in Brantôme
new.desc: Au Fil du Temps is a bistro-style restaurant on chemin du Vert Galant in Brantôme, listed by Gault&Millau.
new.tip: Check opening days on Gault&Millau before going.
new.q: Au Fil du Temps, 1 Chemin du Vert Galant, Brantôme en Périgord
